attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post that the MIT study's results have held strong.

semantics.note: Matches his own description of the MIT finding (5% of companies getting a return) and his claim that it held up. It is a retrospective observation.

contract.note: Asking for comparable later evidence is a fair, ordinary reading of 'held strong'. The result depends on how comparable the denominators and return definitions must be.

evidence.note: The original MIT NANDA report. It is the baseline, not later corroboration. Its 5% figure covers integrated pilots with P&L impact, not all companies.
Wharton survey from Jun–Jul 2025 of large US firms. Its self-reported ROI measure is broader, so it is not comparable enough to contradict the MIT P&L figure.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no later study comparable enough to confirm or refute the roughly 5% finding. The McKinsey material could not be retrieved. Wharton uses a different population and return measure, so it cannot settle the question.

attribution.note: Marcus's own causal assertion in his post.

semantics.note: Faithful. In context, 'results' means business adoption and returns from ChatGPT-style generative AI.

contract.note: Reading 'because' as a material contributing cause, and 'obvious' as publicly documented at launch, is ordinary and fair. A reading requiring unreliability to be the sole cause would be stricter.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch page admitted incorrect answers at launch. This company disclosure works against its own interest and shows the problem was publicly documented from the start.
METR study: experienced developers were 19% slower with AI. Low reliability was linked to wasted time, though this mechanism was observed, not randomised. Narrow population.

BCG survey of professionals: general GenAI tools had modest impact, and lack of accuracy and rework were common. It also names other barriers, so reliability is a contributing cause, not the only one.

reviews.rationale: All three parts of the contract's support condition are met: launch documentation admits unreliability, a deployment study ties it to lost time, and a survey ties inaccuracy and rework to modest gains. Caveats: the populations are narrow, other barriers exist, and there is no economy-wide estimate, so this supports a contributing cause, not the only one.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion about productivity studies.

semantics.note: Faithful. It keeps both parts: some studies show about 30%, and none come close to 10x.

contract.note: Counting task-level studies is fair, since his 30% figure itself comes from task-level studies. The result turns on whether a narrow timing study that compares ChatGPT with physicians counts as a productivity study.

evidence.note: Meta-analysis from May 2025: average gain of about 33% across 20 studies. Supports the 30% part, but an average cannot rule out an individual outlier.

Peer-reviewed 2024 study: ChatGPT-4 produced discharge documents 10x faster than physicians, with quality rated comparable by blinded experts. Narrow task (6 fictional cases), but it meets the contract's contradiction test.
Anthropic disclosure, 2025-11-25: 90% time savings on some tasks, but these are the model's own estimates, not measured worker performance. Context only.

reviews.rationale: The 'about 30%' part holds (e1). The universal 'none have come close to 10x' is contradicted on the contract's task-level reading by a peer-reviewed study reporting 10x faster documents at comparable quality, though that study was a narrow pilot that did not cover whole jobs.

attribution.note: Marcus states this as one of his core beliefs in his own post.

semantics.note: Framed as a core belief he wants made 'absolutely clear', not a hedge. It is a firm, unqualified 'will not' forecast with no deadline.

contract.note: Fair reading of an open-ended negative. It is contradicted only by independently verified AGI from a system within scope. The AGI threshold and the line between LLM and hybrid systems are left unspecified.

evidence.note: ARC Prize, Sep 2026: GPT-6 Astra beats the human baseline on ARC-AGI-3. That is strong benchmark progress, but per the packet the evaluator says it does not establish AGI.
OpenAI's own announcement, Sep 2026, claims state-of-the-art results in many domains. A company disclosure, not independent confirmation of AGI.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and there is no conclusive event: no independently verified AGI from an LLM-based system, and no impossibility result. Benchmark progress and company claims fall short of the early-resolution rule, so the forecast stays open.
